content:
Supervisor: Prof. Dr. Cornelis P. Dullemond

Key Investigations

  • Disk Physics & Evolution: Explored the structure and evolution of protoplanetary and transition disks, focusing on dust–gas decoupling, inner cavities, and observational signatures linked to planet formation processes.
  • Radiative Transfer Modeling: Implemented Monte Carlo radiative transfer simulations using RADMC-3D to compute dust temperature distributions, synthetic images, and spectral energy distributions (SEDs) from physically motivated disk models.
  • Parametric Disk Analysis: Systematically varied disk geometry (inner/outer radii) and stellar mass to quantify their impact on temperature profiles, disk morphology, and spectral characteristics.
  • Synthetic Observables: Generated mid-infrared images and full SEDs to connect theoretical disk structures with observable quantities, highlighting how radiative effects influence interpretation of astronomical data.
  • Warped Disk Modeling: Extended models to fully 3D warped disk geometries, incorporating tilt, rotation, and dynamical perturbations to simulate realistic asymmetries seen in observations.

Outcomes

  • Demonstrated how variations in stellar and disk parameters imprint distinct signatures on temperature structure, morphology, and SEDs—bridging theoretical models with observable disk features.

content:
Supervisor: Dr. Suparna Roychowdhury & Prof. Dhruba Gupta

Key Investigations

  • Stellar Structure & Homologous Modeling: Derived scaling relations for MS stars from fundamental stellar structure equations; Modeled stellar interiors using StatStar, validating theoretical predictions against empirical data.
  • Observational Data Analysis: Analyzed GAIA DR3 and HIPPARCOS surveys to construct Color-Magnitude Diagrams (CMDs) and Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagrams; Identified coeval stars in clusters (e.g., Messier 2) via MIST isochrone fitting, determining age, metallicity, and distance.
  • Post-MS Nucleosynthesis: Studied the triple-alpha process and the critical \(^{12}\text{C}(\alpha,\gamma)^{16}\text{O}\) reaction, which determines the \(\text{C/O}\) ratio in stellar cores; Performed R-matrix analysis (using AZURE2) to resolve resonant energy levels in \(^{16}\text{O}\), enhancing cross-section predictions for helium burning.

Outcomes & Directions

  • Demonstrated observational alignment with homologous models: pp-chain dominates in low-mass stars, while CNO-cycle fits high-mass stars.
  • Quantified uncertainties in \(^{12}\text{C}(\alpha,\gamma)^{16}\text{O}\) rates, pivotal for understanding elemental abundances in evolved stars.
  • Developed Python pipelines for automated isochrone fitting and cluster parameter estimation.
  • Future work involves looking into later evolutionary stages and utilizing more complex evolutionary codes.

content:
Location: Internship at the STARC Lab, Indian Institute of Technology, Indore
Supervisor: Prof. Abhirup Datta
Mentor: Samit Kumar Pal

Key Investigations

  • 21 cm Cosmology & Foregrounds: Investigated the spin-flip hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen (\(1\text{s}\) ground state) emitting \(21\text{cm}\) radiation as a key observational probe of Cosmic Dawn and the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). Analyzed the severe impact of bright astrophysical foregrounds (e.g., galactic synchrotron emission) that obscure this weak signal in radio observations.
  • Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) Framework: Modeled the total observed sky data using custom covariance functions within a Bayesian non-parametric framework. Selected a Squared-Exponential kernel to capture the highly smooth spectral behavior of foregrounds, combined with a non-stationary kernel optimized to isolate the rapidly oscillating cosmic \(21\text{cm}\) signal and instrumental noise.
  • Computational Pipeline: Implemented the GPR framework using the GPy module in Python on synthetic datasets to perform signal-foreground separation.

Outcomes & Directions

  • Successfully extracted the smooth spectral foreground component from the simulated data stream.
  • Current Challenges: The residual cosmic signal remains highly sensitive to noise; further development is required to improve the signal-to-noise ratio (\(\text{SNR}\)).
  • Hyperparameter Sensitivity: Observed that signal extraction is highly sensitive to the initial kernel selection, where variations in covariance structures alter the resulting amplitude metrics.
  • Computational Scaling: Noted that inversion of large covariance matrices scales as \(\mathcal{O}(N^3)\), requiring significant computational overhead for large-scale dataset arrays.

content:
Institution: Xaverian Astronomical Society, St. Xavier’s College, Kolkata
Supervisor: Dr. Suparna Roychowdhury
Contributor: Bipasha Bhattacharjee

Key Investigations

  • Cosmological Parameter Spaces: Investigated the estimation of core parameters governing cosmic expansion dynamics—specifically the Hubble constant (\(H_0\)) and the matter density parameter (\(\Omega_m\))—modeled within a foundational Newtonian cosmology framework.
  • Bayesian Statistical Architecture: Implemented a robust parameter estimation pipeline utilizing a standard Gaussian likelihood function mapped alongside uniform (flat) prior distributions to represent initial parameter uncertainties.
  • Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) Sampling: Utilized MCMC stochastic sampling techniques to efficiently traverse the multi-dimensional parameter space, generating posterior probability distributions and tracing parameter degeneracies.

Outcomes & Directions

  • Successfully derived numerical constraints for both \(H_0\) and \(\Omega_m\) that display strong statistical convergence and align cleanly with established precision observational datasets.
  • Demonstrated the utility and mathematical robustness of Bayesian inference structures for breaking parameter degeneracies in astronomical model fitting.
description: Estimating foundational parameters (\(H_0\) and \(\Omega_m\)) within a Newtonian framework via Gaussian likelihoods and MCMC sampling.
title: Constraining Cosmological Parameters Using Bayesian Inference

Supervisor: Prof. Dhruba Gupta
Mentor: Dr. Kabita Kundalia

Key Investigations

  • Kinematic Core Design: Developed a Python-based computational tool to simulate and visualize kinematic curves for low-energy, two-body nuclear reactions of the form \(A(a,b)B\).
  • Conservation Laws Implementation: Leveraged fundamental energy and momentum conservation laws, incorporating reaction \(Q\)-values and non-relativistic approximations to predict exact energy-angle correlations of secondary reaction products.
  • Experimental Parameters Mapping: Enabled user-defined parameters for all target, projectile, and detector system properties to aid in pre-experimental design and kinematic validation.

Key Simulation Features

  • Stochastic Vertexing: Simulates the exact reaction position and resulting angular distributions using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling arrays.
  • Energy Loss Tracking: Incorporates deterministic energy-loss algorithms tracking particle degradation inside both the target material and active detector media.
  • Multi-Reaction Capabilities: Features a scalable framework capable of overlaying multiple concurrent reactions simultaneously.

Major Tasks & Methodology

  • Particle-Matter Modeling: Simulated full particle-matter interactions in low-to-intermediate energy nuclear reactions using advanced Monte Carlo frameworks.
  • Geometry Configuration: Hand-coded complex, multi-stage detector geometries based on specific exotic nuclei configurations to accurately track physical energy deposition layers.
  • Data Synthesis Frameworks: Utilized specialized computational toolkits including NPTools and GEANT4 to build complete detector environments, tracking simulated reaction outputs for deep analytical evaluation.

Analysis & Optimization

  • Deployed the CERN-ROOT C++ framework to extract, parse, and analyze heavy output simulation trees.
  • Compared synthetic data profiles against established literature baselines to iteratively optimize detector efficiencies.
  • Extracted structural metrics including total reaction cross-sections, optimal input beam energies, and simulated particle tracking counts.

Key Investigations

  • R-Matrix Formalism Optimization: Applied the multi-level, multi-channel R-matrix framework to model resonant scattering behaviors, identifying and characterizing unstable energy levels in compound nuclei appearing as sharp cross-section anomalies.
  • Compound Nucleus Profiling: Conducted comprehensive numerical modeling of the resonant states within the compound nucleus \(^{16}\text{O}\) via the elastic channel \(^{12}\text{C}(\alpha,\alpha)^{12}\text{C}\).
  • Cross-Section Computation: Computed fine-grid differential reaction cross sections mapped strictly against variations in center-of-mass excitation energies using the C++ based AZURE2 configuration platform.
